slides: Now let's see what happens when workers work together.

slides.say: Usually it's two workers, sometimes more. And usually each one has a different rate.
When workers work together, they have one combined rate. Let's see it in numbers.
Dan solves three exercises a minute. Noa solves two exercises a minute.
Together they solve three plus two, five exercises a minute.
at: Together they solve three plus two

slides.say: So to find a combined rate, we add the rates.
Another example. One pump fills eight liters a minute, and another pump fills twelve. Together, eight plus twelve is twenty liters a minute.
Now careful. We add the rates, never the times.
Dan finishes a job in three hours. Noa finishes the same job in six hours. Together, is it nine hours?
at: Dan finishes a job in three hours

slides.say: No. Nine hours is more than Dan needs alone. With help, Dan finishes sooner, not later.
So the times don't add. Only the rates add. In a moment, we'll see how to get the rates from the times.
Sometimes one worker works against the others. Then his rate gets a minus.
I wash five plates a minute. My little brother makes two plates dirty every minute.
at: I wash five plates a minute
My little brother makes two plates

slides.say: So each minute, only five minus two, three plates get clean.
A pipe that fills a tank and a drain that empties it work the same way. The drain gets a minus.
Often the question doesn't say how big the job is. It only says how long the job takes.
Then we call the whole job one. For example, a pump fills one pool in four hours.
The rate is the work divided by the time. So its rate is one over four, a quarter of the pool an hour.
at: So its rate is one over four

slides.say: Let's check it. A quarter of the pool each hour, for four hours, is one whole pool.
at: A quarter of the pool each hour

slides.say: In the same way, a job in five hours means a fifth of the job each hour.
Now let's add rates that are fractions. Pump A fills a pool in four hours. Pump B fills it in twelve hours. They work together.
at: Pump A fills a pool in four hours

slides.say: Pump A's rate is a quarter of the pool an hour. Pump B's rate is a twelfth. So together it's a quarter plus a twelfth.
We need a common denominator, twelve. A quarter is three twelfths. Three twelfths plus one twelfth is four twelfths.
And four twelfths is a third.
at: And four twelfths is a third

slides.say: What does a third mean? A rate is the work over the time. So a third means one pool in three hours.
Another one. A combined rate of two fifteenths means two pools in fifteen hours.
So one pool takes half of that. Fifteen divided by two is seven and a half hours. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
